169.title: Is he mad? (Mark 3:20–30)
169.hook: his family think he's lost his mind; scribes say he's possessed
169.tomorrow: who are my mother and brothers?
169.howItsDone: Christian teaching commonly reads the strong-man picture as Jesus overcoming evil, and some Christians turn to this passage when their own family doesn't understand their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: twelve names, called up into the hills. The word was apostle, one who is sent, and your line was first, to be with him.

Jesus comes into a house, and the crowd packs in so tight that, in the old King James words, they could not so much as eat bread. Word travels. His own people hear what's going on, and they set out to bring him home by force. Mark doesn't soften what they were saying about him. And while they're on the road, visitors arrive from Jerusalem: scribes, with a darker explanation of their own.
screen: `TOO BUSY TO EAT.` → `HIS OWN PEOPLE COME FOR HIM.` → `VISITORS FROM JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, they went to lay hold on him, "for they said, He is beside himself." Out of his mind. The Greek word pictures someone standing outside himself. It's a startling thing for a gospel to include: the people who knew Jesus longest thought he'd lost it. Then the scribes from Jerusalem go further. He has Beelzebul, they say, and he drives out demons by the prince of demons. Jesus doesn't shout. He calls them over and tells them parables. How can Satan cast out Satan? "And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand." If the powers of evil were fighting themselves, they'd be finished already. Then a picture: nobody can rob a strong man's house unless he ties up the strong man first. Christian tradition reads that as Jesus describing what he's doing: tying up evil and taking back what it stole. Then a hard saying about the one sin that won't be forgiven, speaking against the Holy Spirit, and Mark explains it right away: they said he had an unclean spirit. One common Christian reading takes it as calling God's good work evil, so stubbornly that a person won't turn back, and some pastors tell worried people that fearing you've done it is a sign you haven't. And the line traveled. In 1858 Abraham Lincoln borrowed it for a speech about a nation half slave and half free: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Mark's story is also a sandwich: family sets out, scribes accuse, and tomorrow the family arrives.
screen: `HE IS BESIDE HIMSELF.` · `THE SCRIBES SAY: POSSESSED.` · `A HOUSE DIVIDED CANNOT STAND.` · `LINCOLN BORROWED THE LINE IN 1858.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone close got you wrong, someone who should have known better, and notice what comes back with it: the sting, maybe, or the wish to explain. You don't have to win that argument in the next two minutes; you can let it be unfinished. If you pray, bring it to God as it is; if not, let it sit beside you without fighting it.

170.title: Who are my mother and brothers? (Mark 3:31–35)
170.hook: whoever does God's will is family
170.howItsDone: Many Christians call one another brother and sister, and churches often describe themselves as a family of faith, drawing on Jesus's words that whoever does the will of God is his brother, sister and mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, his own people said he was beside himself, and the scribes said Beelzebul, and he answered that a house divided can't stand.

Picture the house: packed wall to wall, people sitting on the floor around Jesus, listening. Outside, at the door, his mother and his brothers, come to bring him home. They can't get in, so they send a message through the crowd, hand to hand, the way you'd pass a note in class. Your mother and your brothers are outside, asking for you. Every head turns to see what he'll do. Most of us know exactly what we'd do. We'd get up. Jesus answers with a question.
screen: `A HOUSE PACKED TO THE WALLS.` → `HIS FAMILY AT THE DOOR.` → `A MESSAGE PASSED IN.`

segments.voice: He asks: who is my mother, or my brethren? Then, in the King James Bible, "he looked round about on them which sat about him, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren!" He looks at the circle on the floor: fishermen, a tax collector, neighbors, strangers. "For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother." Notice the last line. In the King James, the message at the door named his mother and his brothers. His answer adds a sister. The circle keeps getting wider. It can sound cold, turning away his own mother. Christians don't usually read it that way. Most hear the family made bigger, not smaller: the door open to anyone. And they point out that Mary appears again later, near the cross in John's gospel and praying with the disciples in Acts, so she's in the circle too. The brothers raise a question churches answer differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand them as close relatives, cousins, or Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage, holding that Mary remained a virgin. Many Protestants understand them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Both read the same Greek word, brother. And that closes the first part of Mark, three breathless chapters: a voice in the wilderness, the sky torn open, fishermen leaving nets, a man with leprosy, a roof dug through, Levi's table, a withered hand, twelve names, a house divided. It ends here, with a new kind of family sitting on the floor. Next: seeds, storms and loaves.
screen: `WHO IS MY MOTHER?` · `WHOSOEVER SHALL DO THE WILL OF GOD.` · `CHURCHES READ BROTHERS DIFFERENTLY.` · `THE END OF MARK ONE TO THREE.`

Brethren, who Jesus named as he looked around the circle on the floor: whoever does God's will, now called brother, sister and mother too.

171.title: The sower again (Mark 4:1–9)
171.hook: teaching from a boat, he tells of seed thrown everywhere
171.howItsDone: Christians read the sower both on its own and with the explanation Jesus gives a few verses later, and sermons on it often ask what kind of ground a life is today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a message at the door, and Jesus pointing at everyone on the floor: behold my brethren. Your line was family is wider.

The crowd on the shore of the Sea of Galilee is so big that Jesus climbs into a boat, pushes out a little, and sits down to teach from the water, with everyone lined up along the beach. A new part of Mark begins here: chapters four to six, seeds, storms and loaves. And the first thing he says is a single word: listen. Then comes a story you heard on day twenty-three, in Matthew's telling. Today it's Mark's turn.
screen: `A BOAT FOR A PULPIT.` → `MARK FOUR TO SIX BEGINS.` → `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible it starts: "Hearken; Behold, there went out a sower to sow." Hearken means listen, really listen. The farmer walks his field throwing seed by the handful, and it lands everywhere. Some on the hard path, and the birds eat it. Some on rocky ground with a thin skin of soil, where it springs up fast, then scorches and withers in the sun. Some among thorns, which choke it. And some on good ground, where it grows and yields thirty, sixty, a hundred times over. To us the farmer looks careless. Why throw good seed on a path? Some readers suggest he sowed first and plowed the seed under afterward, which would make broad scattering sensible. Either way, this sower doesn't pick and choose. Some Christians hear grace in that: the word is offered to every kind of ground, hard, shallow, crowded and ready. Then Mark closes the story the way he opened it: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." The first word was hearken; the last line is about ears. Everything between is a story about how things are received. Tomorrow the disciples admit they didn't get it, and he explains. For today, notice the parable is wrapped in listening, front and back.
screen: `HEARKEN: THE FIRST WORD.` · `SEED ON EVERY KIND OF GROUND.` · `THIRTY, SIXTY, A HUNDRED.` · `HE THAT HATH EARS TO HEAR.`

segments.voice: Listen outward first: name the farthest sound you can hear, then the nearest, traffic, a fridge, birds, your own breathing. Then listen inward for the quiet thought underneath the busy ones today, and don't answer it; just hear it all the way through, like a seed landing. If you pray, you can offer that listening to God.
Hearken, the first word of the sower's story, meaning listen, really listen: the parable is wrapped in it, front and back.
Your line: let anyone with ears hear. The seed went on every kind of ground. See you tomorrow.

172.title: Why parables? (Mark 4:10–20)
172.hook: the disciples don't get it either, and he explains the sower
172.howItsDone: Many Christians study scripture in small groups where asking what a passage means is expected, and churches often teach the explanation of the sower alongside the parable itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower again, told from a boat and wrapped in hearken, in listening. Your line was let anyone with ears hear.

You're in a class, and the teacher finishes something everyone else seems to follow. Heads nod. You have no idea what just happened. You wait until the room empties, then walk up and say, quietly: sorry, can you explain that? That's today. The crowd thins out, and when he's alone, the twelve, plus a few others who stayed, ask Jesus what the sower story meant. The people closest to him, who'd left their nets and their tax booth for this, didn't get it. Mark doesn't hide that.
screen: `THE CROWD GOES HOME.` → `THE TWELVE STAY BEHIND.` → `WHAT DID THAT MEAN?`

segments.voice: His first answer is a hard passage. He tells them the secret of the kingdom has been given to them, but to those outside everything comes in parables, and he uses words from the prophet Isaiah about people who look and look but don't see, hear and hear but don't understand. It sounds as though stories are meant to keep people out. Christians don't all read it the same way. Some hear it as describing what parables do rather than what Jesus wants: a parable opens up to anyone who leans in and asks, like the twelve did, and stays shut to anyone who walks away. Others read it with Isaiah, whose message was also going to meet closed ears. Then the line that makes Mark so human: "Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?" A little exasperated. A little fond. And he explains. "The sower soweth the word." The path is people who hear it, and at once it's snatched away. The rocky ground is people who take it up with joy but have no root, and fall away when trouble comes. The thorns are "the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things." The good ground hears, takes it in, and bears fruit. So what makes you an insider here? Not being clever. Asking. The ones who got the explanation admitted, out loud, that they didn't understand. In Mark, the disciples will keep not getting it for chapters, and he keeps explaining.
screen: `TO THOSE OUTSIDE, PARABLES.` · `KNOW YE NOT THIS PARABLE?` · `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` · `THE INSIDERS WERE THE ONES WHO ASKED.`

segments.voice: Let something come to mind that you nod along to but don't really get: a part of your faith, or someone else's, how your own money works, why someone you love does what they do, a word everyone at work uses. Say it to yourself plainly, I don't understand this, and notice whether that feels like shame or like relief. If you pray, bring the question to God the way the twelve did, after the crowd left.
Why parables? The disciples' question after the crowd left, and the answer only askers got.
Your line: they didn't get it either. In Mark, the insiders are the ones who asked. Day one hundred seventy-two, done.

173.title: A lamp on a stand (Mark 4:21–25)
173.hook: light isn't meant to hide under a bowl
173.howItsDone: Christians often read the lamp as a call to live their faith openly and to use what they've been given for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve waited till the crowd left and admitted they didn't understand. Your line was they didn't get it either.

It's getting dark in a one-room house in Galilee. Someone fills a small clay lamp with olive oil, lights the wick, and then, very carefully, puts a bowl over it. Or slides it under the bed. Everyone would laugh. That's the joke Jesus tells next, so obvious it sounds silly: nobody lights a lamp to hide it. Lamps are easy. Other kinds of light get hidden more quietly: a gift kept back, a belief never mentioned, a kindness nobody is meant to see.
screen: `A SMALL CLAY LAMP.` → `A BOWL OVER THE FLAME.` → `EVERYONE LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?" Candle there means an oil lamp, a little clay dish with a spout for the wick. A bushel is a grain measure, a household bowl. A candlestick is a lampstand, a ledge or stand that lifts the light so the whole room gets it. The Greek has a small oddity. The sentence literally says: does the lamp come? As if the lamp walked in by itself. Some readers hear Jesus hinting at himself: the light that has come into the room is not meant to stay hidden for long. Then he says nothing is hidden except to be revealed later. After yesterday, it sounds like a promise: what the twelve heard in private is meant to come out into the open. Then a warning about listening, which ties back to the sower: "Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given." Mete means measure out. Whoever pays attention is given more to pay attention to. Christians have taken the lamp two ways, often both at once. Some hear it about the good news, which isn't a secret to hoard. Others hear it about their own lives: whatever light they've been given, faith, a gift, kindness, is meant for the room, not a bowl. Not to show off. Just so people can see.
screen: `A LAMP, A BOWL, A BED.` · `DOES THE LAMP COME?` · `NOTHING HIDDEN FOR LONG.` · `THE MEASURE YOU GIVE.`

Choose one, and picture lifting the bowl and setting that light where someone can see it, not to be admired, just to help the room. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Candle, the King James word for a small oil lamp, never meant to be hidden under a bowl or a bed, but lifted onto a stand.

174.title: Seed growing secretly (Mark 4:26–34)
174.hook: the farmer sleeps and the seed grows, he knows not how
174.howItsDone: Christians often turn to this parable when their efforts seem to show no results, trusting that God gives the growth, and some churches keep old customs of blessing seeds and fields at planting time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a candle lifted out from under the bowl, and a promise: nothing stays hidden for long. Your line was put it on the stand.

A bean in a paper cup, on a classroom windowsill. A kid waters it, then checks it. Every hour. Sometimes the kid digs it up to see if anything is happening, and that's the end of the bean. Grown-ups do a version of it too: checking the email, the scale, the savings, the person they're worried about, the prayer that hasn't been answered. Poking at the soil. Today Jesus tells a very short story about a farmer who does the opposite. He plants, and then he goes to bed.
screen: `A BEAN IN A PAPER CUP.` → `CHECKING EVERY HOUR.` → `A FARMER WHO GOES TO BED.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground; And should sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how." The farmer isn't lazy. He did his part: he planted. But the growing isn't his job, and he doesn't understand it anyway. Then a wonderful little word: "For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself." Of herself, in Greek, is automate: on its own, without help. And it happens in order: "first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear." A green shoot, then a head of grain, then the full grain in the head. You can't skip to the end, and pulling on the blade won't speed it up. Only at harvest does the farmer act again, and then fast, with the sickle. Right after, Mark sets the mustard seed, which you met in Matthew on day twenty-four: the smallest seed, grown into a plant big enough for birds to nest in its shade. Two seed stories side by side, both about what grows beyond what we can see or control. Christian readers hear them as pictures of God's kingdom: it grows quietly, often unseen, and the growing belongs to God. Some also hear patience and trust in ordinary life. You plant. You sleep. Something happens you don't understand. And Mark ends the chapter's teaching by saying Jesus told stories like these as people were able to hear them.
screen: `HE KNOWETH NOT HOW.` · `OF HERSELF — AUTOMATE.` · `BLADE, THEN EAR, THEN FULL CORN.` · `THE MUSTARD SEED, SIDE BY SIDE.`

Picture it as a seed in the dark soil, doing things you can't see, and picture yourself going to bed and leaving it there. If you pray, you can hand it to God for the night; if not, just let the soil hold it.

Your line: it grows while you sleep. The growing was never the farmer's job. That's one hundred seventy-four days.

175.title: Asleep on a cushion (Mark 4:35–41)
175.hook: the storm, the cushion, and the question: who is this?
175.howItsDone: Many Christians pray with this story in times of fear, and peace, be still is a line often said or sung in worship and prayed at bedsides and in hospitals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a farmer slept while the earth bore fruit automate, of itself. Your line was it grows while you sleep.

Evening on the Sea of Galilee. After a long day of teaching from the boat, Jesus says: let's go across to the other side. They push off, and the lake does what it's known for: wind comes down off the hills and whips it up in minutes. Waves break over the side; the boat is filling. Several of these men are fishermen who know this lake, and they're terrified. And Jesus? In the back, asleep. Mark gives one detail nobody else does: his head is on a cushion.
screen: `LET'S GO ACROSS.` → `THE BOAT IS FILLING.` → `HE'S ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish?" Don't you care? That's the real question in a storm. Not just, will we make it? But, does anyone care? Jesus gets up and speaks to the weather the way you'd speak to a barking dog. "Peace, be still." "And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm." A great storm, then a great calm. Then to them: "Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?" The strange part: now they're even more afraid. Mark says they feared exceedingly, and asked each other, "What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" Anyone raised on the Psalms knew who commands the sea. In Israel's scriptures, it's God who stills the storm and quiets the waves. That's the question this whole part of Mark keeps asking: who is this? Christians hear the story in two directions. It's about who Jesus is. And it's about storms of every kind: a diagnosis, a debt, a 3am panic. Many take comfort that the disciples' honest cry, don't you care, is right there in scripture, and that the answer came. That closes a week: a family that thought he was mad, a wider family, the sower from a boat, why parables, a lamp on a stand, a seed growing in the dark, and a man asleep on a cushion in a storm.
screen: `CAREST THOU NOT THAT WE PERISH?` · `PEACE, BE STILL.` · `WHY ARE YE SO FEARFUL?` · `WHAT MANNER OF MAN IS THIS?`

segments.voice: Breathe out longer than you breathe in, and let the thing that's been filling your boat lately come to mind; name it plainly. Picture it as wind and waves around a small boat, with the cushion in the back. If you pray, say the old words from the story, peace, be still, and hand the storm over; if you don't, let each out-breath loosen your grip a little.
Cushion, the detail only Mark kept: Jesus asleep in the back of the boat, his head on a cushion, before the storm and the calm.
Your line: why are you afraid? A great storm, then a great calm. Twenty-five weeks now.

original.note: Greek: something for the head, a cushion. Its only use in the New Testament is here.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about the weather.
what it means: a terrified crew asks don't you care, he calms the sea, and then they're more afraid: who is this?
what a scholar hears: in the Psalms, it's God who stills the sea, so the story's last question points straight at who Jesus is.
recall: a heart gone stiff, like a callus

chat.says: In the storm, the disciples wake Jesus and say 'carest thou not?' What happens next?
options: He calms the sea, asks why they're afraid, and they wonder who this is.
He scolds them for waking him and goes back to sleep on the cushion.
He tells them to row harder, and together they make it through the waves.
